extracted.intended_audience: researchers conducting ML-based scientific studies; journal editors and peer reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and checklist items for documenting, evaluating, and reporting ML-based scientific studies to improve reproducibility, transparency, and validity across the stages of an ML study.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1a) Population or distribution about which the scientific claim is made
rubrics_metrics.description: The population of interest is the group to which the researchers intend the findings of the study to generalize (treated interchangeably with a distribution of scientific interest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the population/distribution clearly because it shapes conclusions, places boundaries on conclusions, and provides the basis for metrics of significance and uncertainty; note that population is typically broader than the sampling frame and sample. Examples and references note that articles often fail to state population clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1b) Motivation for choosing this population or distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why the particular population/distribution was chosen for study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe whether the choice arose from deductive, inductive, or iterative approaches; explicitly communicate the approach used. Explain whether choice was driven by theory, applied need, or data availability, and how that affects interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1c) Motivation for the use of ML methods in the study
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe why ML methods were used rather than (or in addition to) traditional statistical methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain whether the study follows algorithmic modeling (focus on predictive accuracy) versus data-modeling cultures (focus on parameter estimation/causal inference), and why ML is appropriate for the research question; reference debates about interpretability and when algorithmic approaches are preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2a) Dataset (for computational reproducibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report dataset details and cite datasets with permanent links to clarify which version was used; provide documentation for datasets used alongside the study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include data dictionaries or datasheets reporting properties and format. If data are sensitive and cannot be released, consider alternatives (synthetic datasets), but acknowledge limitations since synthetic data may not preserve original data patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2b) Code (version identification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the exact version of code used to run experiments and produce results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a DOI, commit tag, or other precise identifier for code (e.g., Git commit hash) and consider archiving code in repositories that provide permanent identifiers (Dataverse, etc.) to aid long-term reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2c) Computing environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Report hardware and software details required to reproduce computational experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify hardware (CPU, RAM, disk), software (OS, language, package versions), and computing resources (time taken). Follow best practices to document infrastructure so others can reproduce resource requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2d) Documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide user-facing documentation that walks a researcher through setting up and running the code from environment setup to usage examples and expected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good documentation reduces friction for independent researchers: include environment requirements, installation instructions, examples, and expected outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2e) Reproduction script
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a script (or reproducibility container/platform) that can produce all results reported in the paper using the provided materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reproduction script should automate dependency installation (with versions), dataset download/placement, environment setup, and execution to recreate reported results; can be implemented as bash scripts or via platforms like CodeOcean. Acknowledge that full automation may be infeasible for HPC clusters or non-programmatic datasets and provide best-effort alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to provide computational reproducibility materials at time of publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer requiring reproducibility materials (code, data, environment details) at time of publication rather than leaving sharing to post-publication requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence shows post-publication requests often fail; journal standards (e.g., TOP levels) range from stating availability (Level 1) to requiring verified materials (Level 3). When one aspect (e.g., private data) cannot be met, provide other artifacts (reproduction script, synthetic data, clear documentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: 3a) Data source(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe when, where, and how data were collected and, if applicable, how ground-truth annotations were performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sufficient detail so readers can evaluate strengths/weaknesses and appropriateness for study goals; reviews show reporting of data-source details and annotation methods varies and is sometimes insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3b) Sampling frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the sampling frame (the list of units from which the sample was drawn) and eligibility criteria for inclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify boundaries of the sample and how it relates to the target population; note that many papers omit clear sampling-frame descriptions or make them hard to find.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3c) Justification for why the dataset is useful for the modeling task
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why the chosen dataset is appropriate for answering the research question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific about dataset strengths/limitations (not just 'best dataset available'); for repurposed 'big data', use known characteristics to justify suitability and identify shortcomings; discuss how biases or incompleteness affect the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3d) Outcome variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe precisely how the outcome/target variable is defined and measured, and provide descriptive statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat outcome as an empirical proxy for a theoretical construct; note mismatches and potential fairness issues; report descriptive stats to reveal rare values or skewness.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3e) Number of samples in the dataset
rubrics_metrics.description: Report total sample size and, for classification tasks, the number of samples in each class; distinguish individuals versus rows when applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss adequacy of sample size relative to objectives (e.g., rare events, heterogeneity). Warn that large sample size with unrepresentative sampling can give false confidence; report subgroup sizes and post-attrition sample counts where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3f) Missingness
rubrics_metrics.description: Report prevalence of missing data and indicate how missingness was handled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Missing data is prevalent and can bias results; specify patterns of missingness and handle nonrandom missingness carefully. (Note: specific handling methods are covered under data transformations item 4c.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 3g) Dataset for evaluation is representative
rubrics_metrics.description: Justify that the evaluation dataset is representative of the target population defined in Module 1, or explain limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representativeness supports generalizability; probability sampling is one approach but not always necessary—compare sample characteristics to population or use statistical adjustments (post-stratification, propensity weighting) when appropriate; note that nonrepresentative data may be acceptable for within-sample comparisons but must be discussed under external validity (Module 8).

rubrics_metrics.name: 4a) Excluded data and rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Report which samples were excluded from analysis and justify the rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The subset of data used determines the scope of claims; justify exclusions (e.g., outliers, focusing on subsets) because choices can substantially affect model performance and conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4b) How impossible or corrupt samples are dealt with
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe detection and handling of impossible or corrupted data points (e.g., impossibly large values, bot responses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report methods used to detect such cases and whether data were removed or transformed; relate to excluded-data reporting (4a) and transformations (4c).

rubrics_metrics.name: 4c) Data transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Report preprocessing transformations applied to the data (e.g., normalization, augmentation, imputation, resampling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify when and how imputations or resampling were done (e.g., perform imputation/oversampling separately within each fold) because improper preprocessing can cause overoptimistic results and harm validity; preprocessing choices affect reproducibility and model properties like accuracy and interpretability.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5a) Model description
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide specific details about all models trained, including inputs/outputs, model type (e.g., Random Forest, Neural Network), loss function, and training algorithm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exact model specification is essential for reproducibility; many papers lack sufficient detail to reproduce models from text alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5b) Justification for the choice of model types implemented
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why the selected set of model types was appropriate for the study's scientific claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice depends on goals (e.g., predictive accuracy vs. interpretability for high-stakes settings); acknowledge debates (e.g., interpretability) and provide reasons for including or excluding certain model types.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5c) Model evaluation method
rubrics_metrics.description: Report details of the model evaluation procedure (how data were split and used: holdout, external validation, nested cross-validation, etc.) and sample sizes per split (including class counts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation must be done on data separate from training and model selection; report split strategy and sizes to ensure reproducibility and validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5d) Model selection method
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe how final model(s) were selected from candidate fitted models (including hyperparameter choices and selection criteria).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid improper selection (e.g., choosing the best model after testing on the holdout set) which inflates performance estimates; use separate test sets or nested CV; discuss predictive multiplicity and alternative selection criteria beyond accuracy (fairness, interpretability).

rubrics_metrics.name: 5e) Hyperparameter selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Report how hyperparameters were searched and selected, and document the impact of hyperparameter choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyperparameter search affects performance and comparisons; provide search strategy and note variance in performance across hyperparameters, which may bias comparisons between methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5f) Appropriate baselines
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare models to appropriate, well-tuned baselines and detail how baselines were trained and optimized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure baselines use comparable model selection and optimization procedures to avoid 'weak baseline' artifacts that overstate new-method benefits; supplement with appropriate statistical tests when comparing models (see item 7c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Module 6: Data leakage (identify and prevent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect and avoid spurious relationships between features and target arising from data collection, sampling, preprocessing, or modeling (leakage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give concrete examples (e.g., normalizing features across train+test creates leakage); recognize leakage is common and can arise at multiple pipeline stages—document steps taken to detect and prevent it and explain how preprocessing and evaluation practices avoid leakages.
